lessons.title: wir, ihr, sie: all the pronouns, and hobbies
lessons.goal: Say what you, your friends and other people do in your free time, with the right verb ending.

grammar.point: wir and sie (they) take -en; ihr takes -t; the other endings stay the same
grammar.oneLine: wir -en, ihr -t, sie (they) -en. Hobby verbs: spielen, hören, kochen.

mistake.why: ihr takes -t. Only wir and sie (they) take -en.

terms.meaning: we: you and other people together
you, when you talk to two or more friends
more than one other person
what you like to do in your free time

cards.title: Before we start: we, you all, and they
cards.body: Chapter 2, Freunde, Kollegen und ich, is about friends, colleagues and yourself, over three study days. A real moment: a friend asks what you do in your free time. Today you learn to say what we, you all and they do.
steps: You already know: du wohnst and er wohnt from chapter 1, with the endings -st and -t.
New today: wir, ihr and sie with their endings, plus hobby verbs such as spielen.
By the end you can: say Wir spielen Fußball and Ihr spielt Tennis.

examples.why: You know this: du + -st, from chapter 1.
New today: wir takes the ending -en.

cards.more: Think of the endings as name tags on a verb. You met the tags for ich, du, er, sie and Sie in chapter 1. Today there are three more tags. Wir means we: you and other people together. Ihr means you when you talk to two or more friends. Sie can mean they, and it takes the same tag as the polite you: -en. Why does this matter? The verb is the same word for the whole group, so the tag tells the listener who is doing the action. The full table comes in the next cards, and you practise it on hobbies step by step.

cards.title: wir: we
cards.body: wir means we: me and other people. wir takes the ending -en. The verb is still in position 2.
cards.more: wir means we: you plus other people, like a group photo. The tail is -en. It is the same ending as the full verb: wohnen gives wir wohnen. Step 1: say wir. Step 2: take the verb in the form that ends in -en. Step 3: done. Extra example: Wir kochen. = We cook.
cards.lead: In chapter 1 you learned ich and du, and how the verb changes for each person. On this card: the word wir for we, and its ending, so you can talk about yourself and other people.

cards.title: ihr: you (two or more friends)
cards.body: du is one friend. ihr is two or more friends. ihr takes the ending -t. Use ihr when you talk to a group of friends.
cards.more: Think of a classroom. If the teacher looks at one friend, she says du. If she looks at the whole group, she says ihr. English only has one word, you, for both. German has two. For ihr, glue -t to the stem: spiel + t. It is the same ending as er and sie (she). So spielt can mean ihr spielt or er spielt. The pronoun tells you who it is.
cards.lead: You know wir now. Next: the word for talking to a group of friends, so you can speak to two or more people you know well with the right verb.

cards.title: sie: they
cards.body: sie with a small s can mean she or they. They takes -en. She takes -t. More than one person means they. Names joined with und are they.
cards.more: Look at the verb ending to know which sie it is. Ending -t: one woman, she. Ending -en: many people, they. Big Sie with -en is you, polite. A trick: if you can swap in a name, one name means -t (Mira kocht). Two names or more means -en (Mira und Ben kochen). The verb tells the truth, so check it every time.
cards.lead: You can speak to a group now. On this card: the small word sie, which can mean she or they, and how the verb tells you which one is meant.

cards.title: All six endings in one table
cards.body: Learn the whole set. Look at the two columns: spielen and hören. Only the pronoun and the ending change. The stem stays.
cards.more: Think of a verb as a toy with a swappable tail. The stem is the body. Only the tail changes with the person. Step 1: find the stem: spiel-. Step 2: pick the tail from the table. Good news: er/sie and ihr both take -t, and wir and sie/Sie both take -en. So there are only four tails to learn. Extra example: Wir hören Musik. = We listen to music.
cards.lead: You have met the endings one at a time. Next: all six forms of two verbs side by side, so you can compare them and see the pattern at a glance.

cards.title: One small change: tanzen
cards.body: The stem of tanzen is tanz-. It already ends in an s sound (z). So du gets only -t: du tanzt, not du tanzst. You know this from heißen: du heißt.

examples.why: tanz- ends in an s sound: only -t.

cards.more: Say tanzst out loud. It is hard. Two s sounds in a row: z and s. German avoids it. The z is already an s sound, so the extra s is dropped. That is why the du form looks the same as the er form: tanzt. The same happens for heißen. Rule: if the stem ends in an s sound (s, ß, z), du takes only -t. For all other verbs, du takes -st.
cards.lead: You now have all six endings. On this card: one verb with a small exception, tanzen, which means to dance, so you can use it correctly with du.

cards.title: Find the form in 3 steps
cards.body: When you are not sure, use these steps. They work for every verb in this lesson.
cards.more: Think of a recipe. Step 1: take off -en to get the stem: kochen gives koch. Step 2: ask who it is. Step 3: add the tail for that person. Example: schwimmen gives schwimm, then ihr gives schwimmt. Say it out loud, it gets easy fast. Extra example: Wir kochen. = We cook.
cards.lead: You know all six endings and tanzen. Last card of this lesson: three steps to find the right verb form, so you can use the same method on verbs you have not seen yet.

lessons.title: sein and haben: all six forms
lessons.goal: Use sein and haben with every person, and say you are hungry, thirsty or tired.

grammar.point: sein and haben are irregular: learn all six forms by heart
grammar.oneLine: sein: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind. haben: habe, hast, hat, haben, habt, haben.

mistake.why: In German you have hunger. Hunger and Durst go with haben.

terms.meaning: a verb that does not follow the stem + ending pattern
one spelling of the verb, for one person: habe, hast, hat

cards.title: Before we start: sein and haben, all six
cards.body: A real moment: at a café you say Ich habe Durst. I am thirsty. German does not say am here. It says you have thirst. Today you learn haben and the full sein, all six forms, so you can say how you feel.
steps: You already know: ich bin, du bist, er ist and Sie sind from chapter 1.
New today: haben (habe, hast, hat, haben, habt) and the rest of sein (wir sind, ihr seid).
By the end you can: say Ich habe Hunger and Wir sind nett.

examples.why: You know this: ich bin from chapter 1.
New today: haben, not sein, goes with Hunger.

cards.more: Think of haben and sein as two toolboxes. Sein is for being: your name, who you are, and how you are. Haben is for having: time, hunger and thirst. English says I am hungry, but German says I have hunger, so Hunger, Durst and Zeit go with haben. Why? That is simply how German works, so learn the pairs together. Both verbs are irregular, so they do not follow the endings from chapter 1. You learn all six forms by heart, one row at a time. Each row gets a short table in the next cards.

cards.title: haben: to have
cards.body: haben means to have. It is irregular: some forms break the pattern. du hast (not habst). er/sie hat (not habt). Learn all six.

examples.why: du hast. Literally: you have thirst.

cards.more: Most verbs: stem + ending. For haben the stem is hab-. Two forms lose the b: hast and hat. Why? The b dropped out over time. You just need to remember the three odd ones: du hast, er/sie hat, ihr habt. The others (habe, haben, haben) look normal. Practice by saying: ich habe, du hast, er hat.
cards.lead: You can talk about yourself and others with wir, ihr and sie. Next: haben, the verb for to have, which breaks the usual pattern, so you learn its six forms as one set.

cards.title: Say what you have: Hunger, Durst, Zeit
cards.body: Zeit means time. Hunger means hunger. Durst means thirst. In German you have them: Ich habe Hunger. Do not say am. These words come without a or the.
cards.more: In English you are hungry. In German you have hunger, like holding it in your hand. So never say Ich bin Hunger. Step 1: say Ich habe. Step 2: add Hunger, Durst or Zeit. There is no a or the in front. Extra example: Du hast Durst. = You are thirsty.
cards.lead: You know haben now. On this card: the words for hunger, thirst and time, which go with haben, so you can say you are hungry or that you have time.

cards.title: sein: all six forms
cards.body: You know ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, Sie sind. Now the rest: wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind. sein is irregular. Learn it by heart.
cards.more: sind is used three times: wir sind, sie (they) sind and Sie (polite) sind. So there are only five different words for six people. ihr seid is the odd one. It is not seind and not sind. It is seid. To remember: seid ends in d, like the English word 'said'. Say the whole row out loud with a rhythm: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind.
cards.lead: You can say what you have. Next: the other key verb, sein, with all six forms, so you can say how you feel and where you are.

cards.title: sein or haben?
cards.body: English says I am hungry. German says Ich habe Hunger. Hunger and Durst take haben. müde (tired) and krank (sick) take sein. Check the list.
cards.more: In English, hungry is a feeling word, so you say I am hungry. In German, Hunger is a thing, a noun, that you have. It is like saying I have a cold. müde is a describing word, like nice. Describing words go with sein. Nouns that you have go with haben. A fast test: can you say 'I have ...' in English? Then it is probably haben.
cards.lead: You now know sein and haben. On this card: how to pick the right one for a feeling, like being tired or sick, so your sentences say exactly what you mean.

cards.title: Names are pronouns too
cards.body: A name works like a pronoun. Ben = er. Mira = sie (she). Two names joined by und = sie (they). The verb matches the pronoun.
cards.more: A name is a pronoun in disguise. Ben is the same as er, so use the verb for er: ist, hat. Mira is the same as sie, so also ist, hat. Anna und Leon is the same as sie (they), so use sind, haben. Step 1: swap the name for a pronoun in your head. Step 2: pick the verb. Extra example: Ben und Mira sind müde. = Ben and Mira are tired.
cards.lead: You know how each pronoun takes its verb. Last card of this lesson: how a name, such as Ben, or two names together, works in the same way, so you can talk about other people.

lessons.title: Yes/no questions, ja or nein, and gern
lessons.goal: Ask friends yes/no questions about hobbies and say what you like to do.

grammar.point: A yes/no question starts with the verb; gern comes after the verb and the person
grammar.oneLine: Verb first: Spielst du Tennis? Ja, ich spiele gern Tennis.

mistake.why: The question starts with the verb, and the verb must fit du.

terms.meaning: a question you answer with ja or nein
gladly: it says you like to do something

cards.title: Before we start: yes/no questions and gern
cards.body: A real moment: a friend asks, Spielst du gern Gitarre? Do you like to play guitar? You want to answer yes and say what you like to do. Today you learn gern (gladly) and how to answer ja or nein with a full sentence.
steps: You already know: yes/no questions with the verb first, like Sprichst du Deutsch?
New today: gern right after the verb, and ja or nein with a full sentence.
By the end you can: ask Spielst du gern …? and answer Ja, ich spiele gern.

examples.why: You know this: the verb comes first, from chapter 1.

examples.en: Yes, I like to play tennis.
examples.why: New today: gern comes right after the verb.

cards.more: Think of a yes/no question as a flip. Take a statement and move the verb to the front, and it becomes a question. Ja or nein answers it, and you can add a short sentence after the comma. Gern is a small word that means gladly. In a statement it sits right after the verb, like a friend sitting next to it. In a question it sits after the person: Spielst du gern …? Why? German keeps gern in the same spot each time, so you can build the sentence step by step: verb, gern, then the hobby. The next cards practise one step at a time.

cards.title: Yes/no question: the verb goes first
cards.body: A yes/no question has no question word. You answer it with ja or nein. The verb moves to position 1. The person comes after it. The verb form fits the person.
cards.more: A statement is like a train with the verb in the second car: Du spielst Tennis. To turn it into a question, swap the first two cars: Spielst du Tennis? Only the order changes. The words stay the same. English adds a helper word (do you play?). German has no helper. It simply puts the verb in front. Say the question with your voice going up at the end.
cards.lead: In chapter 1 you asked yes or no questions with sprechen. Next: the same word-order move, now with hobby verbs, so you can ask a friend what they do.

cards.title: Answer: ja or nein + a full sentence
cards.body: You can answer with ja or nein only. Or add a full sentence after it. After ja or nein comes a comma. Then the verb is in position 2 again.
cards.more: ja or nein is like a nod. Then comes a comma, a small breath. Then the sentence goes on as normal. The nod stands outside the sentence, so the verb is still in position 2, right after ich. Step 1: nod with ja or nein. Step 2: comma. Step 3: a full sentence. Extra example: Nein, wir spielen Tennis. = No, we play tennis.
cards.lead: You can ask a yes or no question now. On this card: how to answer with ja or nein and a full sentence after it, so your reply sounds natural.

cards.title: Ask the right person
cards.body: The verb changes with the person you ask. A friend: du. Two friends: ihr. Someone polite: Sie. A third person: er, sie or a name.
cards.more: Think of a key for each person. The verb tail must fit whom you ask. Step 1: a friend? du, tail -st. Step 2: two friends? ihr, tail -t. Step 3: polite? Sie, tail -en. In a yes/no question the verb goes first. Extra example: Spielt Mira Tennis? = Does Mira play tennis?
cards.lead: You know how to answer. Next: how the question changes depending on who you ask, one friend, two friends, a polite person or someone else, so you use the right verb.

cards.title: gern: like to
cards.body: gern means gladly. It says you like to do it. Put gern after the verb and the person. Verb in position 2. Examples: Ich spiele gern Tennis.

examples.en: I like to listen to music.

cards.more: gern is a little smile word. It says you enjoy it. English uses like to, German uses a small extra word. Step 1: make a normal sentence. Step 2: slip gern in right after the verb and the person. Nothing else moves. Extra example: Ben schwimmt gern. = Ben likes to swim.
cards.lead: You can ask what people do. On this card: the small word gern, which means gladly, so you can say that you like doing something.

cards.title: Ask what someone likes: Spielst du gern …?
cards.body: Put gern in a question too. Same place: after the verb and the person. Add a hobby at the end.

examples.en: Do you like to play guitar?

cards.more: Same smile word, now in a question. Think of a sandwich with four layers: verb, person, gern, hobby. Step 1: start with the verb. Step 2: add the person. Step 3: add gern. Step 4: add the hobby. To answer, copy the layers into a statement. Extra example: Hörst du gern Musik? = Do you like to listen to music?
cards.lead: You can say what you like to do. Next: how to ask a friend what they like doing, with gern in the question, so you can start a conversation about hobbies.

cards.title: What do you like to do? Was machst du gern?
cards.body: was means what. machen means to do or to make. A W-question: was is position 1, the verb is position 2. Answer with a hobby sentence.

examples.en: What do you like to do?

cards.more: was means what, and it opens a W-question just like wie and wo. Step 1: was is position 1. Step 2: the verb is position 2. Step 3: add the person and gern. To answer, use any hobby you know with gern. Extra example: Was macht Mira gern? – Mira tanzt gern. = What does Mira like to do? – Mira likes to dance.
cards.lead: You can ask about hobbies with gern. Last card of this lesson: the question word was, which asks what someone likes to do, so you can ask a wider question about free time.

lessons.title: The days of the week: am Montag, and wann?
lessons.goal: Name the days, say on which day you do something and ask someone for a day.

grammar.point: am + day = on that day; the verb stays in position 2 even when the day comes first
grammar.oneLine: Am Montag spiele ich Tennis. The verb is part 2; the subject goes after it.

mistake.why: The verb stays in position 2. The subject goes after it.

terms.meaning: one of the seven days: Montag, Dienstag, …
a small word like am or in that goes before a noun
the first part of the sentence; it does not have to be the subject

cards.title: Before we start: days of the week and am
cards.body: A real moment: a friend asks, Hast du am Freitag Zeit? Do you have time on Friday? To answer, you need the days of the week and the word am. Today you learn all seven days and how to say on which day you do something.
steps: You already know: haben forms such as habe and hast, from lesson 2.
New today: the seven days, am + day, and wann (when).
By the end you can: answer Ja, am Freitag habe ich Zeit.

examples.why: You know this: haben, from lesson 2.
New today: am + day comes first, and the verb stays part 2.

cards.more: Think of a week as seven boxes, and each day as a label you stick on a sentence. Am means on, so am Freitag means on Friday. Six days end in -tag, and Mittwoch is the odd one out. Why does the verb stay put? German keeps the verb in part 2 even when the day moves to the front. So the day becomes part 1, and the subject moves to after the verb. Step by step: pick the day, put am before it, then build the sentence with the verb in second place. The next cards let you build one sentence for each day.

cards.title: Seven days
cards.body: The week has seven days. Six end in -tag. Mittwoch is the odd one out. Learn them in order. Days have a capital letter, like all German nouns.
cards.more: Seven days make a rhythm, like a song. Six of them end in -tag, and Tag means day. Mittwoch is the odd one out. (Mitte = middle, Woche = week: the middle of the week.) Step 1: say all seven in order. Step 2: spot the -tag ones. Step 3: remember Mittwoch is the middle. Days always start with a big letter. Extra example: Samstag, Sonntag = Saturday, Sunday.
cards.lead: You now talk about hobbies and ask questions. Next: the days of the week in order, so you can talk about when things happen in your week.

cards.title: am + day = on that day
cards.body: am Montag means on Monday. Use am before every day. am + day is one part of the sentence.
cards.more: am is a sticker that means on. Pin it to a day, like a calendar entry. am Montag means on Monday. Step 1: say am. Step 2: add the day. The two words are one block. Extra example: Ich koche am Sonntag. = I cook on Sunday.
cards.lead: You know the seven days. On this card: how to say on a day, using a small word before the day name, so you can say when you do something.

cards.title: wann? = when?
cards.body: wann is a question word. It asks for a time. Answer a wann question with am + day. A W-question: wann is position 1, the verb is position 2.
cards.more: wann is the clock question. It asks for a time, and today the answer is a day. Step 1: wann is position 1. Step 2: the verb is position 2. Step 3: add the person. Answer with am + day. Memory help: wann, wo and woher all start with w. Extra example: Wann kochst du? – Am Sonntag. = When do you cook? – On Sunday.
cards.lead: You can say on a day now. Next: the question word for asking when something happens, and how to answer it, so you can ask a friend when they have time.

cards.title: Start with the day: the verb stays second
cards.body: You can put the day first. Then the day is part 1. The verb stays in position 2. The subject now comes after the verb. Same words, new order.

examples.why: Day first, verb second, then ich.
morgen first, then bin, then ich.

cards.more: Think of the sentence as a row of chairs. The verb always sits on chair number 2. Chair 1 can be anyone: the subject, or a day. If you put am Montag on chair 1, the subject ich has to move. It sits down behind the verb, on chair 3. The meaning stays the same. Only the order changes. A common mistake is to keep ich on chair 2. Then the verb sits on chair 3, and that is wrong.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer with when. On this card: how to put the day at the front of a sentence, and where the verb stays while the words move around.

cards.title: Arrange to meet

cards.title: Before we start: verbs that change their vowel
cards.body: A real moment: at a restaurant you say Ich esse Pizza, but your friend says Du isst Kuchen. Some verbs change their vowel for du and er/sie. Today you learn which verbs do this, and when the change happens.
steps: You already know: sprechen changes e to i for du (du sprichst), from chapter 1.
New today: essen and treffen (e to i), and lesen and sehen (e to ie).
By the end you can: say Du isst Kuchen and Mira sieht Ben.

examples.why: You know this: sprechen changes e to i for du, from chapter 1.
New today: essen changes e to i for du.

cards.more: Think of some verbs as having a wobble in the middle. For most people the vowel stays steady, but for du and er/sie it wobbles: e becomes i, or e becomes ie. Why? It is a stem change, and it only happens for those two people. The endings stay the same as before: -st and -t. Step by step: check that the verb is on the list, check the person is du or er/sie, then change the vowel and add the ending. The lists are short, so the next cards help you learn them by heart.

cards.title: Stem change: only du and er/sie
cards.body: You know sprechen: ich spreche, du sprichst. The e becomes i for du and er/sie. All other persons keep the e. The endings stay the same.
cards.more: Look at the six persons. Only two of them change the vowel: du and er/sie. The other four keep it. Draw a box round the du and er/sie rows. Inside the box the e becomes i. Outside the box nothing changes. Easy test: is the person du or er/sie? Then change the vowel. If not, keep the stem as it is. The endings are the normal ones you know.
cards.lead: You know sprechen and its vowel change. Next: the rule for which people get the change, so you can use the same pattern with other verbs too.

cards.title: essen: e → i
cards.body: essen means to eat. du and er/sie get i. The new stem is iss-. It ends in an s sound, so du takes only -t: du isst.
cards.more: Say essen with du: essst? Too many s. German drops one: du isst. This is the same rule as du heißt and du tanzt: if the stem ends in an s sound, du gets only -t. So du isst and er isst are the same word. ihr is different: ihr esst, with the normal e, because ihr does not change the vowel.
cards.lead: You know when a vowel changes. On this card: essen, which means to eat and changes its vowel for two of the people, so you can say what you eat.

cards.title: treffen: e → i
cards.body: treffen means to meet. du and er/sie get i: du triffst, er trifft. Use it with a name or a pronoun after the verb.
cards.more: treffen has a hidden gear. Only du and er/sie shift it: e becomes i. Everyone else stays on e. Step 1: take the stem: treff-. Step 2: for du or er/sie change e to i: triff-. Step 3: add the tail: -st or -t. So du triffst, er trifft. Extra example: Wir treffen Ben. = We meet Ben.
cards.lead: You now know essen. Next: treffen, which means to meet and follows the same vowel change, so you can say who you meet.

cards.title: lesen and sehen: e → ie
cards.body: lesen means to read. sehen means to see. The e becomes ie for du and er/sie. The stem lies- ends in an s sound: du liest. sehen: du siehst.
cards.more: Two different changes happen here. First, e becomes ie: the stem lies- and sieh-. The ie is a long vowel sound, like the e in see. Second, with lesen the new stem lies- ends in an s sound, so du takes only -t: liest. With sehen the stem sieh- ends in h, so du takes normal -st: siehst. Just learn: du liest, du siehst, er liest, er sieht.
cards.lead: You have seen the i change twice. On this card: two verbs with a different vowel change, to read and to see, so you can tell the two changes apart.

cards.title: Spot it in 3 steps
cards.body: Is the verb on the list? Is it du or er/sie? Then change the vowel and add the ending.
cards.more: Use this like a checklist. Step 1: is the verb one of essen, treffen, lesen, sehen? If not, nothing special. Step 2: is it du or er/sie? If not, no change. Step 3: change the vowel, then add the tail. ich, wir, ihr and sie stay normal. Extra example: Du siehst Ben. = You see Ben.
cards.lead: You now know three groups of verbs. Last card of this lesson: three steps to spot which verbs change their vowel, so you can check a verb before you use it.

lessons.title: a → ä and the extra e: fahren, schlafen, arbeiten, and jobs
lessons.goal: Use verbs with an umlaut change or an extra e, and say where you work and what your job is.

grammar.point: Some verbs change a to ä for du and er/sie; stems ending in -t add an extra e

cards.title: Before we start: fahren, schlafen and arbeiten
cards.body: A real moment: a new colleague asks where you work, and you say Ich arbeite als Koch. Some verbs change a to ä, and some need an extra e. Today you learn both patterns, plus job words for a man and a woman.
steps: You already know: essen changes e to i, so du isst, from the last lesson.
New today: a to ä for fahren and schlafen, and an extra e for arbeiten and warten.
By the end you can: say Du fährst nach Wien and Ich arbeite als Koch.

examples.why: You know this: essen changes e to i for du.
New today: fahren changes a to ä for du.

cards.more: Think of fahren and schlafen as verbs with a small hat that appears on the a for du and er/sie. The hat is only there for those two people. Arbeiten and warten are different: their stem ends in t. For du, er/sie and ihr you add an extra e before the ending, so the t and the ending do not run together. Why? Without the e, the word is hard to say. Step by step: find the verb, check the person, then either change a to ä or add the extra e. Each pattern gets its own card next, with examples and a small table.

cards.title: fahren: a → ä
cards.body: fahren means to drive or to travel. For du and er/sie the a becomes ä. This is a stem change, like essen. ich, wir, ihr, sie keep the a.
cards.more: It is the same box idea as before. Only du and er/sie change. Before the change was e to i. Now it is a to ä. An umlaut is a vowel with two dots. Say ä like the e in bed. fährst sounds like 'fairst'. Find the umlaut in the table: it sits only in the du and er/sie rows. nach means to, and you use it with cities: nach Hamburg.
cards.lead: You can spot a vowel change now. Next: fahren, which means to drive, and a different vowel that changes for some people, so you can say where you drive.

cards.title: schlafen: a → ä
cards.body: schlafen means to sleep. It follows the same pattern as fahren. du schläfst, er schläft. The ending is normal: -st and -t.
cards.more: Same idea as fahren. For du and er/sie, a gets two little dots: a becomes ä. Think of a hat that only two persons wear. Step 1: stem: schlaf-. Step 2: for du or er/sie: schläf-. Step 3: add -st or -t. The others get no dots. Extra example: Er schläft gut. = He sleeps well.
cards.lead: You know fahren. On this card: schlafen, which means to sleep, and it follows the same change, so you can say how much you sleep.

cards.title: The extra e: arbeiten, warten
cards.body: arbeiten means to work. warten means to wait. The stem ends in t. For du, er/sie and ihr we add an extra e. Then you can say it: du arbeitest.
cards.more: Try saying arbeitt out loud. You cannot. Two t sounds are stuck together. So German adds a small e to give your mouth a break: arbeitet. The same happens with warten: wartet. The extra e shows up in three places: du, er/sie and ihr. ich, wir and sie (they) have no problem, because their endings already start with a vowel.
cards.lead: You know two kinds of vowel change. Next: verbs whose stem gets an extra e, arbeiten and warten, so the endings are easier to say and to spell.

cards.title: When do you need the extra e?
cards.body: Look at the end of the stem. If it ends in -t, add the extra e for du, er/sie and ihr. Verbs on this list: arbeiten and warten.

examples.why: wart- ends in t: extra e.
arbeit- ends in t: extra e.

cards.more: Say arbeitst out loud. The t and the st crash into each other. German adds a tiny e as a speed bump: arbeitest. Step 1: does the stem end in -t? (arbeit-, wart-) Step 2: is it du, er/sie or ihr? Then add e before the tail. ich, wir and sie get no extra e. Extra example: Du arbeitest hier. = You work here.
cards.lead: You have seen the extra e in arbeiten and warten. On this card: how to tell when a verb needs it, by looking at how its stem ends.

cards.title: Jobs: Ich arbeite als …
cards.body: als means as. Ich arbeite als Koch means I work as a cook. A woman's job ends in -in. Remember: no word for a before a job. Some jobs get an umlaut: Arzt, Ärztin.

examples.en: He works as a shop assistant.

cards.more: A job is like a name tag, so there is no little word for a in front. Ich bin Koch is enough. als means as. For a woman, add -in. Sometimes dots appear too: Arzt becomes Ärztin. Step 1: say the man's job. Step 2: for a woman add -in. Step 3: check for dots. Extra example: Mira arbeitet als Lehrerin. = Mira works as a teacher.
cards.lead: You can use arbeiten now. On this card: how to say what job you do, with als, and the job words for a man and a woman, so you can talk about work.

cards.title: Review: which change?

cards.more: Four switches. Each one only works for certain verbs. Step 1: is the verb on the list? Step 2: is it du or er/sie? Only they get the vowel change. Step 3: for stems ending in -t, add the extra e. ich, wir and sie stay normal. Extra example: Er fährt. Er arbeitet. = He drives. He works.
cards.lead: You have learned the patterns one by one. Last card of this lesson: all four changes side by side, so you can see which pattern each verb follows.

lessons.goal: Learn nouns with their article der, die or das and use them in short sentences.

grammar.point: Every noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das): learn the article with the noun
grammar.oneLine: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch. er, sie, es.

mistake.why: Tisch is masculine. It takes der. Learn the article with the noun.

terms.meaning: a naming word for a person, a thing or a place: Mann, Tisch, Hamburg
a small word before a noun: der, die, das (the)
the group of a noun: masculine, feminine or neuter

cards.title: Before we start: der, die or das?
cards.body: A real moment: a shop assistant says, Der Tisch ist neu. The table is new. Every German noun comes with a little article: der, die or das. Today you learn that nouns come in three groups, and how to use the right article.
steps: You already know: er and sie from chapter 1, for he and she.
New today: der, die and das, and es for things.
By the end you can: say Der Tisch ist neu. and Das Buch ist neu. Es ist super.

examples.why: You know this: er ist from chapter 1.
New today: Buch is a das noun, so it takes das.

cards.more: Think of nouns as members of three teams: the der team, the die team and the das team. Each noun has one team, and its article is the team badge. English has one word, the, but German shows the team every time. Why does it matter? The badge also decides the pronoun: der Tisch becomes er, die Lampe becomes sie, and das Buch becomes es. Step by step: learn each noun with its article, then pick er, sie or es to match. The next cards give tips for guessing the team, and practise each one.

cards.title: Every noun has a gender
cards.body: A noun is a naming word: Mann, Tisch, Buch. Every German noun belongs to a group: masculine, feminine or neuter. This is called its gender. It has nothing to do with real men or women. A table is masculine.
cards.more: Think of three coloured boxes: blue, red and green. Every noun lives in one box. The box has a little word on its lid: der (blue), die (red) or das (green). You cannot guess which box from the meaning. A table is blue, a lamp is red, a book is green. It is like a name tag. The easy way is to learn the tag with the noun. Do not learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.
cards.lead: You now know the endings for many verbs. Next: nouns, the naming words, and the idea that each one belongs to a group, so you can learn their articles.

cards.title: der, die, das = the
cards.body: English has one word for the: the. German has three: der, die, das. They are articles. The article shows the gender. Always say the article with the noun.
cards.more: English has one tool for the: the. German has three buckets: der, die, das. Every noun lives in one bucket. You cannot see which one from outside, so learn the noun and its article together, like a name with a number. Step 1: say the noun. Step 2: put the article in front. Extra example: Das ist das Handy. = That is the phone.
cards.lead: You know that nouns have groups. On this card: the three words for the, and why you say the word with every noun, so you never leave it out.

cards.title: Say what something is like
cards.body: Put the noun with its article first. Then ist, then a describing word. neu means new. You know nett and super too.
cards.more: Use three parts in order. Part 1: the noun with its article. Part 2: ist. Part 3: a describing word, like a sticker. It is the same pattern as Frau Weber ist nett in lesson 5. Step 1: der Tisch. Step 2: ist. Step 3: neu. Extra example: Die Lampe ist neu. = The lamp is new.
cards.lead: You can say the article with a noun. Next: how to describe a thing with ist and a short word like neu, so you can say what something is like.

cards.title: Guess the gender: two tips
cards.body: Two tips help. Nouns ending in -in are always die: Lehrerin. Many nouns ending in -e are die: Lampe, Tasche. But not all. Always check.
cards.more: These are detective clues for the gender. Clue 1: the end -in means a woman, so always die. Clue 2: the end -e is often die, but not always. Step 1: look at the end of the noun. Step 2: -in? die. Step 3: -e? Probably die, but check. Other endings: check in a list. Extra example: die Studentin = the student (woman).
cards.lead: You can describe things now. On this card: two clues that help you guess a noun's article before you check, so you can learn new words faster.

cards.title: er, sie, es: he, she, it
cards.body: A pronoun can stand for a thing. der Tisch becomes er. die Lampe becomes sie. das Buch becomes es. Use er, sie or es to match the gender.

cards.title: Before we start: more than one thing
cards.body: A real moment: a shop has many lamps and books, and you say Die Lampen sind neu. The lamps are new. Today you learn to talk about more than one thing. Plural nouns always take die, but their endings vary.
steps: You already know: der, die, das and ist, from the last lesson.
New today: plural nouns take die and sind, with five ending patterns.
By the end you can: say Die Tische sind neu and learn each noun with its plural.

examples.why: You know this: der Tisch with ist, from the last lesson.
New today: the plural takes die and sind, and the noun gets a plural ending.

cards.more: Think of one table and a pile of tables. Singular means one thing, and plural means more than one. For the pile, the article always becomes die, and the verb changes from ist to sind. Why? The verb must match the number of things. The ending on the noun changes too, but there is no single rule for it, so German has five patterns. Step by step: learn each noun with its article and its plural, like a pair of shoes that go together. The next cards show each pattern with examples, so you can recognise them.

cards.title: Plural: die + sind
cards.body: Singular means one. Plural means more than one. In the plural every noun takes die. The verb changes too: sind, not ist. The noun gets a plural ending.
cards.more: Imagine the three boxes from the last lesson: blue, red and green. When you have many things, they all go into one new box: the plural box. Its lid says die for everything. So der Tisch, die Lampe and das Buch all become die in the plural. The noun itself also changes at the end. And the verb changes: one thing is, many things are. ist becomes sind.
cards.lead: You know der, die and das for one thing. Next: what changes when there is more than one, and the word die you use for many things, so you can talk about several things.

cards.title: Plural pattern 1: add -n or -en
cards.body: Many feminine nouns add -n or -en. Nouns ending in -e add -n. Others add -en. Feminine nouns are the most regular.
cards.more: Plural just means more than one. Pattern 1 gives feminine nouns a tail. Step 1: does the noun end in -e? Add -n. Step 2: if not, add -en. Step 3: the article becomes die. Extra example: Das sind die Lampen. = Those are the lamps.
cards.lead: You know the plural word die. On this card: the first plural pattern, an ending of -n or -en, which many feminine nouns follow.

cards.title: Plural pattern 2: add -e
cards.body: Many masculine nouns add -e. Some also get an umlaut on the vowel: der Stuhl → die Stühle.
cards.more: Many masculine nouns add -e. Sometimes dots appear on the vowel too, because it is easier to say. Step 1: is it a masculine noun from the list? Step 2: add -e. Step 3: some also get dots, so learn each one. The article becomes die. Extra example: Das sind die Tische. = Those are the tables.
cards.lead: You have one plural pattern. Next: a second one with -e, common for many masculine nouns, and the case where a vowel changes too.

cards.title: Plural pattern 3: add -er
cards.body: Some neuter nouns add -er. If the vowel is a, o or u, it gets an umlaut. das Buch → die Bücher.
cards.more: This pattern has two helpers: add -er, and put two dots on the vowel if it is a, o or u. Buch has a u, so Buch becomes Bücher. Mann has an a, so Mann becomes Männer. Kind has an i, and i never gets dots, so Kind becomes Kinder. Dots only go on a, o and u. Check the table: three nouns, three changes.
cards.lead: You know the -e plural. On this card: the -er plural, which some neuter nouns use, and the vowel change you need to watch for.

cards.title: Plural pattern 4: add -s
cards.body: Some nouns add -s. These are mostly words from other languages: Handy, Auto, Hotel.
cards.more: Words that came from other languages often take -s, like in English: phones, cars. Step 1: is it a word from another language? Step 2: add -s. Step 3: the article becomes die. Extra example: Das sind die Autos. = Those are the cars.
cards.lead: You know three plural endings. Next: the -s plural, which mostly appears in words borrowed from other languages, so you can spot them quickly.

cards.title: Plural pattern 5: no change
cards.body: Some nouns do not change. Many end in -er: der Lehrer → die Lehrer. Only the article changes: der becomes die.
cards.more: Some nouns need no tail, because they already end in -er. Nothing is added. Only the article changes: der becomes die. Step 1: does the noun end in -er? Step 2: keep the noun as it is. Step 3: change the article to die. Extra example: Die Lehrer sind nett. = The teachers are nice.
cards.lead: You have four plural endings. Next: nouns that stay the same in the plural, where only the article changes, so you know there is nothing to add.

cards.title: Learn three things per noun
cards.body: There is no safe rule for the plural. So learn each noun with three things: the article, the noun and the plural. Write it down like this.
cards.more: Think of a contact in your phone: name, number, address. A noun also needs three things: article, singular and plural. There is no safe rule for the plural, so learn it with the noun. Step 1: learn der Tisch. Step 2: learn die Tische. Step 3: say both out loud. Extra example: das Auto, die Autos = the car, the cars.
cards.lead: You know five plural patterns. Last card of this lesson: why you learn three things for each noun, the article, the noun and its plural, so you never have to guess.

lessons.title: Numbers from 20, age, and filling in a form
lessons.goal: Say numbers up to 1000, tell your age and fill in a short form.

grammar.point: Numbers over 20 are said backwards: einundzwanzig = one-and-twenty

mistake.why: The one comes first, then und, then the ten.

terms.meaning: the last digit of a number: 1 to 9
20, 30, 40 …: zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig

cards.title: Before we start: numbers, age and forms
cards.body: A real moment: a form asks, Wie alt bist du? How old are you? You need to write your age and your phone number in the boxes. Today you learn numbers over 20 up to 2000, the age question, and the labels on a form.
steps: You already know: Wie heißt du? and the verb sein from chapter 1.
New today: numbers over 20 with und, Wie alt bist du? and the form labels.
By the end you can: say your age and fill in a short form.

examples.why: You know this: a W-question from chapter 1.
New today: numbers over 20 say the one first, then und, then the ten.

cards.more: Think of a big number like a sandwich with two layers. The unit goes first, then und sits in the middle, and the ten goes last. Twenty-five is fünfundzwanzig: five, and, twenty, all in one word. That is why German numbers sound backwards to English speakers. Why? It is just how the word is built, so learn the small parts first: zero to twenty, then the tens, then the big numbers. Forms work the same way: read the label, then write your answer in the box. The next cards show each step with a number, then the age question, then a short form.

cards.title: Numbers 0 to 20: the base
cards.body: First the base. You need these to build bigger numbers. Learn them in rows. 13 to 19 end in -zehn.
cards.more: Numbers 0 to 20 are Lego bricks. All bigger numbers are built from them. 0 to 12 are separate words, so learn them one by one. 13 to 19 are built: unit + zehn, like three-ten. Watch two changes: sechzehn loses the s, siebzehn loses the en. Step 1: learn 0 to 12. Step 2: build 13 to 19. Extra example: vierzehn = vier + zehn = 14.
cards.lead: You know how nouns and their plurals work. Next: the numbers from 0 to 20, which you need as the base for every bigger number.

cards.title: The tens: 20, 30, 40 …
cards.body: The tens end in -zig. Three are odd: 30 is dreißig with ß. 16 is sechzehn but 60 is sechzig. 17 is siebzehn but 70 is siebzig.
cards.more: Compare sechzehn (16) and sechzig (60). Both start with sech-. 16 has -zehn at the end. 60 has -zig. Same with siebzehn (17) and siebzig (70): siebzehn has -zehn, siebzig has -zig and the -en of sieben falls out. Listen for zehn (teen) or zig (ty). That is the same idea as English: sixteen and sixty. Say each pair out loud.
cards.lead: You know the numbers up to 20. On this card: the tens, 20, 30, 40 and so on, with a few tricky spellings to learn by heart.

cards.title: 21 to 99: say the one first
cards.body: German says the one first, then und, then the ten. It is one word. 21 is one-and-twenty: ein + und + zwanzig. The word for 1 is ein here, not eins.
steps: Then und, then the ten: vierzig
cards.more: English says twenty-one: ten first. German says one-and-twenty: the one first, like in an old rhyme: four-and-twenty blackbirds. Build it from the end of the number backwards. 53: the 3 comes first, drei. Then und. Then the ten, fünfzig. Write it as one word: dreiundfünfzig. For 1 use ein, so 21 is einundzwanzig. Check: 47 is siebenundvierzig, not vierundsiebzig, which is 74.
cards.lead: You can say the tens now. Next: how to join a small number to a ten, such as 21 or 45, so you can say numbers up to 99 in one word.

cards.title: 100 and 1000
cards.body: hundert is 100. tausend is 1000. Say the bigger number first, then the rest, all in one word: 125 is hundertfünfundzwanzig. 2000 is zweitausend.
cards.more: Big numbers are glued into one long word, with no spaces. Step 1: say the big part first: hundert. Step 2: add the rest right after it. Step 3: write it as one word. Extra example: hundertzehn = hundert + zehn = 110.
cards.lead: You can count to 99. On this card: the words for 100 and 1000, and how a big number is written as one long word, so you can read prices and years.

cards.title: Age: Wie alt bist du?
cards.body: wie alt means how old. Ask: Wie alt bist du? Answer: Ich bin … Jahre alt. Jahre means years. Learn Jahre alt as a chunk. Use sein for age.
cards.more: Age uses sein, like in English: I am 25. German adds Jahre alt, years old, as a block. Step 1: ask Wie alt bist du? Step 2: answer Ich bin + number + Jahre alt. Never use haben for age. Extra example: Mira ist zwanzig Jahre alt. = Mira is 20 years old.
cards.lead: You can say big numbers now. Next: how to ask someone's age and answer it, with sein and the word Jahre, so you can say how old you are.

cards.title: A form: what goes where
cards.body: A form asks for facts. Learn the labels. Vorname is your first name. Nachname is your last name. You write them in boxes.
cards.more: A form is a set of labelled boxes. The label tells you which fact goes in. Step 1: read the label. Step 2: write that fact. (Vor = before, Nach = after: Vorname comes first, Nachname comes last.) Extra example: Beruf: Lehrerin = Job: teacher.
cards.lead: You can say your age now. Last card of this lesson: the labels on a German form, such as Vorname and Alter, so you know what to write in each box.
